Theme

scarecrow noun

also scarecrows, bird scarer

classical

Liv. 34.11.7: nūllīs minīs, nūllīs terriculīs sē mōtōs (Lewis & Short)
Liv. 5.9.7 (Lewis & Short)
M-O s.v. scarecrow

terricula, terriculōrum n. pl.

noun, second declension, plural

things to frighten with: a scarecrow, a bugbear

From terreō; very rare, and in Livy of empty threats (Lewis & Short). Morgan–Owens gives the singular terriculum for a scarecrow.

Other words

  • formīdō, formīdinis f. — a terror; a thing set up to scare

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Hor. S. 1.8.3–4: fūrum aviumque maxima formīdō; M-O s.v. scarecrow

    Horace’s garden Priapus calls himself “the great terror of thieves and birds”.

Examples

  • deus inde ego, fūrum aviumque maxima formīdō

    so I am a god, the great terror of thieves and birdsHor. S. 1.8.3–4

See also garden, bird, crow, frighten.

SourcesLewis & Short: terricula · Lewis & Short: formido

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. scarecrow.

Horace, Sermones 1.8.3–4.
